## How to reproduce this file

Render from the repository root (`_quarto.yml` sets `execute-dir: project`, so
every path below is relative to the project root, not this folder):

```
quarto render assignments/assignment05-visualization/submission/visualization-audit.qmd
```

Rendering re-reads `examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv` and
re-exports `corrected-plot.png` into this submission folder.

## Setup

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

nhanes <- read_csv("examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(nhanes)
```

## Part 1: Audit of the flawed plot starter

`flawed-plot-code.R` compares mean BMI by income group at the first and last
NHANES cycle only. Reproducing its logic here (without the `ggsave`/file-path
block, which is just a run helper) to see what it actually shows:

```{r}
cycle_levels <- sort(unique(nhanes$Cycle))
endpoint_cycles <- c(cycle_levels[1], cycle_levels[length(cycle_levels)])

flawed_summary <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), Cycle %in% endpoint_cycles) |>
  group_by(Cycle, IncomeGroup) |>
  summarise(mean_bmi = mean(BMI), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

flawed_summary
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Flawed plot as written by the starter script."
flawed_plot <- ggplot(
  flawed_summary,
  aes(x = Cycle, y = mean_bmi, color = IncomeGroup, group = IncomeGroup)
) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line(linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(24, 28)) +
  labs(
    title = "Low income drives rising obesity in American adults",
    subtitle = "Adults age 20-80: BMI climbed steadily across every NHANES cycle",
    x = "NHANES cycle",
    y = "BMI",
    color = "Income"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

flawed_plot
```

**Issues found in the flawed starter** (see `visual-audit-note.md` for the
full table):

1. **Causal title.** "Low income drives rising obesity" claims causation from
   a cross-sectional, unweighted, descriptive comparison.
2. **Age claim does not match the code.** The subtitle says "Adults age
   20-80," but the pipeline never filters on `Age`. The summary silently
   includes every age in the file (`r min(nhanes$Age)`-`r max(nhanes$Age)`),
   including infants and children, under a title about "American adults."
3. **Truncated y-axis.** `scale_y_continuous(limits = c(24, 28))` starts well
   above zero, which visually doubles the apparent gap between income groups.
4. **Only 2 of 11 cycles shown, but captioned as "every... cycle."** Using
   only the endpoint cycles and drawing a line between them manufactures a
   "steady climb" that the two points alone cannot demonstrate.
5. **Missingness dropped silently.** `filter(!is.na(IncomeGroup))` removes
   `r sum(is.na(nhanes$IncomeGroup))` rows with no missingness count reported
   anywhere in the plot or caption.

## Part 2: My own initial draft

My descriptive question: **how does mean BMI differ by household income
group in the most recent NHANES cycle?** First pass, before the audit:

```{r}
draft_summary <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), Cycle == "2021-2023") |>
  group_by(IncomeGroup) |>
  summarise(mean_bmi = mean(BMI), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

draft_summary
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "My initial draft, before the audit."
draft_plot <- ggplot(draft_summary, aes(x = IncomeGroup, y = mean_bmi, fill = IncomeGroup)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(25, 31)) +
  labs(
    title = "Low income Americans have higher BMI",
    x = "Income group",
    y = "Mean BMI"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

draft_plot
```

**Issues I found in my own draft:**

6. **Zoomed bar-chart axis.** `coord_cartesian(ylim = c(25, 31))` makes a
   ~2-point difference in mean BMI look like a tall/short bar comparison
   instead of a small relative difference.
7. **Population-level title.** "Low income Americans have higher BMI"
   generalizes an unweighted classroom sample to the whole country; NHANES
   sample weights (not used here) are what would let a claim like that
   extend beyond the sample.
8. **No age restriction and no sample size shown.** Like the flawed starter,
   this draft includes every age in the file, and a reader cannot see how
   many people are behind each bar or how many rows with missing income were
   dropped.

## Part 3: Revised, corrected plot

The revision: restrict to adults aged 20-80 (so "BMI by income group" is not
mixing in pediatric growth-related BMI), show **all 11 cycles** instead of
two endpoints, start the BMI axis at 0, drop the causal/population framing,
and report the sample sizes behind the lines.

```{r}
adults <- nhanes |> filter(Age >= 20, Age <= 80)

corrected_summary <- adults |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup)) |>
  group_by(Cycle, IncomeGroup) |>
  summarise(mean_bmi = mean(BMI), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

n_dropped <- nrow(adults) - nrow(adults |> filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup)))
n_total_adults <- nrow(adults |> filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup)))

tibble(adults_age_20_80 = nrow(adults),
       dropped_missing_bmi_or_income = n_dropped,
       analyzed = n_total_adults)
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Corrected plot: full axis, all cycles, descriptive framing, sample sizes stated."
corrected_plot <- ggplot(
  corrected_summary,
  aes(x = Cycle, y = mean_bmi, color = IncomeGroup, group = IncomeGroup)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 32), breaks = seq(0, 32, 8)) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean BMI by household income group, NHANES 1999-2023",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Descriptive and unweighted; adults aged 20-80 (n = ", n_total_adults, ")"
    ),
    x = "NHANES cycle",
    y = "Mean BMI (kg/m^2)",
    color = "Income group",
    caption = paste(
      strwrap(
        paste0(
          "Source: classroom NHANES snapshot, examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv (CDC/NCHS). ",
          "Excludes ", n_dropped, " adult records missing BMI or income group, and all ages outside 20-80. ",
          "Descriptive, unweighted sample statistics; not survey-weighted or population-representative, ",
          "and not evidence that income causes BMI differences."
        ),
        width = 95
      ),
      collapse = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 8),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1)
  )

corrected_plot

ggsave(
  "assignments/assignment05-visualization/submission/corrected-plot.png",
  corrected_plot, width = 9, height = 6.5, dpi = 150
)
```

## Interpretation

Across all 11 NHANES cycles in this classroom snapshot, adults (20-80) in the
lowest household income group have a higher mean BMI than middle- and
high-income adults in every cycle shown, and the gap between the low-income
and high-income lines is wider in the most recent cycles than in 1999-2000.
This is a **descriptive, unweighted** pattern in this sample only: NHANES
sample weights were not applied, so these numbers describe the people
measured in this classroom file, not the U.S. population, and a cross-
sectional comparison like this cannot show that income differences cause the
BMI differences.

## Connection to Assignment 4

The `IncomeGroup`, `BMI`, and `Age` columns and the unweighted/descriptive
caveat used here are the same ones checked for parity in
[Assignment 4](../../assignment04-polyglot/submission/polyglot-parity.qmd),
which is why the missingness counts for `IncomeGroup` and `BMI` match what
was reported there.
